name: Mayi-Kutuna
confidence_why: No published description states where Mayi-Kutuna puts word stress: the only account, Breen 1981, describes initial stress for Ngawun, which Breen himself treats as a separate, mutually unintelligible language, and mentions Mayi-Kutuna only for its sound patterns, so any placement for Mayi-Kutuna would be a guess by analogy.

catalog_quote: [§2.3, p. 25, Ngawun phonology:] The main stress on a word is almost always on the first syllable. Occasionally there is a secondary stress on the second syllable of a trisyllabic word. In a four-syllable word there may be a secondary stress on the third syllable, especially if the word is a reduplicated form. In a longer word secondary stress tends to fall on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, if any (for example [íkalamùndʊ] 'grass-ABL'), or otherwise on odd-numbered non-final syllables (e.g. [wánatʸùŋkaṛi] 'moon'). ... The word /puṛiŋkir/ 'tomorrow' is exceptional in that the main stress frequently falls on the second syllable, the first vowel then being centralised to [ə] and often reduced, thus [pəríŋkər]. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the §2.3 passage is verbatim on the page image we hold of Breen 1981 p. 25 and the §2.5 passage is verbatim in the text we hold layer of p. 29; §2.5 mentions Mayi-Kutuna only for phonotactics and never for stress, so 'undetermined' (no stress statement for this languoid; the only Mayabic stress statement is Ngawun's) is a faithful reading. The deciding source is the only description that exists (Glottolog: sole descriptive ref; Austlang G24 downloaded now via the Internet Archive: grammar 'on Ngawun', Breen 1981 'mainly on Ngawun'), so no better published source is being missed. The residual risk is internal to Breen 1981: we hold 10 of 238 pages, and ch. 1 plus any Mayi-Kutuna notes are unreached; Austlang confirms tape/field-note material for G24 exists, so Breen may have had audio and could have remarked on stress elsewhere in the book. That makes the record adequate rather than well-so
